## Formula (Suppose the t-th annual growth rate is g_t, expressed in decimals; n=5)

1. Arithmetic average annual growth rate:
   \(\bar g = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n} g_t\), multiplied by 100 when expressed in %.
2. Five-year CAGR:
   \(CAGR = \left(\prod_{t=1}^{n}(1+g_t)\right)^{1/n}-1\), multiplied by 100 when expressed as %.
3. Compound cumulative growth from the end of 2018 to the end of 2023:
   \(Cum = \prod_{t=1}^{n}(1+g_t)-1\), multiplied by 100 when expressed in %.
4. Naive sum:
   \(S = \sum_{t=1}^{n} g_t\), multiplied by 100 when expressed in %.
5. Sum minus actual compound cumulative (percentage points):
   \(S - Cum\) (both in %, difference in percentage points).
6. Arithmetic mean minus CAGR (percentage points):
   \(\bar g - CAGR\) (both in %, difference in percentage points).

## Why is the arithmetic mean not equal to CAGR?

The arithmetic average averages the annual growth rates themselves and ignores compound interest: it treats each year's growth as an increment relative to the same starting point. CAGR answers "If compound interest grows at the same rate every year, what is the rate that can reach the same terminal value from the beginning to the end of the period?" It is determined by the ratio of the levels at the beginning and the end of the period, and is the growth rate in the geometric mean sense. Since the product of \((1+g_t)\) is generally not equal to \((1+\bar g)^n\) (unless the growth rates in each year are exactly the same), the two are usually not equal; the greater the growth rate fluctuations, the more obvious the difference is usually.

## Why annual growth rates cannot be added directly to get cumulative growth

Cumulative growth is the change in the final value relative to the beginning level: \(Cum=\prod(1+g_t)-1\). Direct addition \(\sum g_t\) is equivalent to adding every year's growth to the same starting point, ignoring the compound interest effect of "the growth base becomes larger year by year". The naive summation is approximately equal to the compound accumulation only when the annual growth rates are small and fluctuate; in general the summation will systematically deviate (usually overestimation, if the growth rate is positive and fluctuating, the cross term \(\sum_{i<j}g_i g_j\) is missed). The difference \(S-Cum\) is exactly the magnitude of these compound interest cross terms.
